title: Why Ships Have Two Colours
coreQuestion: Why is the bottom of a ship's hull painted differently?

facts.claim: Anti-fouling paint is applied as the outer layer to the hull of a ship to slow the growth of subaquatic organisms that attach to the hull.
Those organisms can affect a vessel's performance and durability.
Anti-fouling coatings belong to the underwater hull paints, also known as bottom paints.
In antiquity, copper plates and lead plates were used to protect the underwater hull.
Anti-fouling paints are used to coat the bottoms of ships to prevent sealife such as algae and molluscs attaching themselves to the hull, slowing down the ship and increasing fuel consumption.
The convention prohibits the use of harmful organotins in anti-fouling paints used on ships.

narration.text: Why is the bottom of a ship painted a different colour?
That lower coat is a working paint, called bottom paint.
Underwater, tiny organisms try to attach themselves to the hull.
Anti-fouling paint slows their growth on the hull.
Left alone, they can affect a ship's performance and durability.
Long before modern paint, shipbuilders protected the underwater hull with copper or lead plates.
The colour line marks where the fight against the sea's hitchhikers begins.
